fed-treasury-accord-and-william-mcchesne.context_blurb:
For almost nineteen years, from 1951 to 1970, William McChesney Martin Jr. ran the Federal Reserve, America's central bank, longer than anyone else has. He is remembered for one image, a party and a bowl of punch, and for the harder thing behind it: telling presidents no when they wanted cheap money.

The story begins in the Second World War. To keep Washington's borrowing cheap, the Fed pinned interest rates low, buying up as many government bonds as it took and in effect creating new dollars to lend to the Treasury. When the war ended and price controls came off, all that new money was still in circulation, and prices rose as too many dollars chased the same supply of goods.

Even after the war the Fed stayed tied to the Treasury's needs. The Treasury-Fed Accord of March 4, 1951, finally gave the central bank back its power to set interest rates by itself. Economists draw a lesson from the episode: in wartime a central bank surrenders its independence to paying the government's bills, and winning that independence back afterward is a political fight that has to be fought openly, never simply assumed.

There was a twist. Martin had helped negotiate the Accord as a Treasury official, arguing the Treasury side. So when President Harry Truman chose him to chair the Fed in April 1951, Truman expected a loyal ally. Instead Martin became a fierce defender of the Fed's independence, and Truman felt betrayed.

Martin had grown up inside the system. When the Fed opened for business in 1914, the first governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis was Martin's own father, who bore the same name, and thirty-seven years later the son took charge of the whole system. He went on to serve five presidents in a row: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon.

In October 1955 Martin addressed a gathering of investment bankers in New York and found the image that defined him. The Fed, he said, is like the chaperone who orders the punch bowl carried away at the very moment the party is starting to warm up. The punch stood for cheap credit, the easy money that makes a boom feel lively. Martin meant that the Fed must cut off the easy money before the boom can end in a crash.

Financial writers turned his line into shorthand for a particular job: restrictive monetary policy, imposed during a boom and against political pressure, lifting rates to calm an economy running too hot. That is also why the job is so hard. Tightening is always unpopular at the moment it matters most, because it arrives exactly when everyone is enjoying the good times.

Martin felt that pressure in the late 1960s. President Lyndon Johnson paid for the Vietnam War and his Great Society programs at once without raising taxes to cover them, while the Fed kept rates low enough to keep government borrowing cheap. A country that combines big unfunded spending with cheap central-bank money tends to get high inflation a few years later, and the Great Inflation of the 1970s, which Martin's successor Arthur Burns made worse, followed.

frederic-bastiat-the-journalist-economis.context_blurb:
Frederic Bastiat was a French farmer, journalist and politician who wrote economics for ordinary readers. In just six years, from 1844 until his death in 1850, he produced the essays that still teach people to hunt for the unseen costs of every policy. He was born in Bayonne in 1801, lost both parents young, and was raised by his grandfather on the family estate at Mugron in southwestern France.

For some twenty years Bastiat farmed at Mugron and read deeply about trade and money, hardly known beyond his district. Then, in October 1844, the Journal des Economistes, the Paris flagship of the French free-trade school, printed his article comparing English and French tariffs, and almost at once he was famous.

Across the Channel, Britain's Corn Laws kept bread dear for the poor by loading foreign grain with heavy duties. The Anti-Corn Law League, which Richard Cobden and John Bright had launched in Manchester in 1838, fought those duties with rallies, pamphlets and speeches; it was a free-trade movement of national reach, and in 1846 it won repeal. Bastiat visited England, befriended Cobden and went home to build a French version.

Bastiat wrote in plain, lively French that ordinary working people could follow. He refused, on purpose, the mathematical formalism of equations and graphs, wanting every reader to check each step of an argument without algebra; wit, stories and satire were his tools instead.

After the revolution of 1848 toppled King Louis-Philippe, Bastiat won a seat in the Assembly the revolution created, kept it in the election that followed, and served on its finance committee. In speech after speech he went after the socialists of Louis Blanc and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, whose national workshops and free-credit bank he believed would ruin France.

In the summer of 1850, already gravely ill with tuberculosis, he sent two short works to the printer within weeks of each other. La Loi, The Law, came out in June, and in July came Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas, the essay on what is seen and what is not seen.

The second holds his most famous story. A boy breaks a shop window, and onlookers cheer that at least the glazier will get work. Bastiat pointed to the sale nobody sees: the shopkeeper must now spend his money on glass, so he cannot buy the new shoes he intended, and the shoemaker loses that sale.

Judging every choice against the alternative given up is what modern textbooks call opportunity cost, and they credit Bastiat with its first clear statement. Together with the broken window, it is his lasting gift to economics.

Bastiat hoped to be remembered for something larger: Harmonies economiques, his reply to the socialists, meant to prove that free exchange breeds cooperation instead of class war. Only the first part appeared before he died, and the remainder was pieced together afterward from his notes.

That autumn his doctors sent him south for the mild Italian winter. He went first to Pisa and then on to Rome, and there, on Christmas Eve, 1850, he died at forty-nine; he lies buried in the French church of San Luigi dei Francesi. His friend Prosper Paillottet, who was at the bedside, reported that in his last hour Bastiat kept murmuring two words, "la vérité, la vérité," the truth, the truth. His friends took the phrase as the summary of a life spent refusing to lie about consequences.

friedrich-hayek-who-he-was.context_blurb:
Friedrich Hayek was born in Vienna in 1899 and died in Freiburg, Germany, in 1992, and in between he lived through the century's great contest between planned economies and free ones. More than anyone, he explained why the planners kept failing. His answer was not mainly a moral one. It was about knowledge: what it is, and where it lives.

As a young economist in 1920s Vienna, Hayek went to the private seminar that Ludwig von Mises ran every second Friday at the Chamber of Commerce, where Mises worked, and he always credited Mises with teaching him real economics.

In 1931 Lionel Robbins invited Hayek to London to give four lectures. Published as Prices and Production, they laid out his theory of the business cycle, the claim that booms built on cheap central-bank credit are bound to collapse into busts. The lectures went so well that the London School of Economics gave him a chair, which he held until 1950.

While German bombs fell on London, Hayek wrote The Road to Serfdom, published in 1944 for British and American readers, and it became a bestseller in both countries. Its warning was that a government trying to direct an entire economy from above, however kind its intentions, slides step by step toward controlling more and more of ordinary people's lives, because every plan needs someone to enforce it.

In 1947, with central planning fashionable everywhere, Hayek brought about forty classical-liberal scholars together at a resort high above Lake Geneva. They founded a society named after the mountain, the Mont Pelerin Society, to keep the free-market tradition alive.

In 1950 Hayek moved to the University of Chicago, but its economics department would not hire him. Chancellor Robert Hutchins found him a professorship elsewhere, on the interdisciplinary Committee on Social Thought, paid for by the William Volker Fund.

His central idea is the knowledge problem. A modern economy runs on millions of scraps of local knowledge, about what is wanted, what is scarce and what things cost, scattered in millions of heads, and no committee, however brilliant, can ever gather them in one place. Market prices carry that knowledge instead. In 1974 Hayek shared the Nobel Prize in Economics with Gunnar Myrdal.

In his prize lecture in Stockholm that December he took aim at his own field. His fellow economists, he said, had borrowed the trappings of physics, its formulas and confident forecasts, without the knowledge that would justify them. He called the lecture The Pretence of Knowledge.

His final book, The Fatal Conceit, appeared in 1988, when he was eighty-nine. In it he argued that morality, the family, property and markets evolved over countless generations into an order too intricate for any planner to rebuild. The fatal conceit, in his phrase, is the confidence that human reason can design from a blank page what took history ages to evolve.

Hayek also refused to call himself a conservative. In "Why I Am Not a Conservative," the postscript to his 1960 book The Constitution of Liberty, he found "libertarian" an unattractive label too and preferred to stand with the Old Whigs. What his tradition defends is the conviction that prices, laws and customs grew up over centuries and cannot be redesigned from nothing.

gordon-tullock-the-lawyer-who-co-founded.context_blurb:
Gordon Tullock, born in Rockford, Illinois, in 1922, helped found one of the most important ideas in modern economics without ever earning a doctorate in the subject. He was a lawyer and a diplomat first. What he saw inside real governments convinced him that politicians and officials respond to incentives like everyone else.

Tullock took a law degree at the University of Chicago in 1947 and then spent nearly ten years in the US Foreign Service, posted in Tianjin during the Communist takeover of China, in Hong Kong and in Korea. He later said those years of watching officials scheme and bargain taught him more about how political incentives work than any economics class ever could.

That insight became a whole branch of economics. It treats officials, legislators and the citizens who elect them as self-interested human beings who want votes, larger budgets and promotions, not as saints serving the common good, and it is called public choice, or public-choice economics. A mayor who puts promised new parks in swing districts, where grateful voters can reward him, rather than in the poor neighborhoods that need them most, is behaving exactly as public choice predicts.

In 1958 Tullock joined James Buchanan at the University of Virginia, and in 1962 the two published The Calculus of Consent, the book that launched the field. In 1966 Tullock started the field's own journal, first called Papers on Non-Market Decision Making and renamed Public Choice in 1968, and he edited it for more than thirty years.

In 1965 Tullock turned the same tools on government offices in The Politics of Bureaucracy, showing how officials build careers, enlarge their agencies and defend their turf; William Niskanen's 1971 study of bureaus built directly on it. The head of a government office usually wants more staff, prestige and power, so year after year he asks for a bigger budget, even when its workload is falling. Offices like his try to grow, and almost never volunteer to shrink.

In 1967 Tullock described another hidden cost of government. When the state hands out a few valuable permits that let only certain firms do business, companies pour money into lobbying for the permits instead of into better products, and all that effort creates nothing. Anne Krueger, studying India's import licenses in 1974, gave the behavior its modern name: rent-seeking.

Tullock even applied the tools to dictatorship, in a 1987 book. A dictator, he and later thinkers such as Bruce Bueno de Mesquita argued, does not need to please the masses. He needs to keep a narrow circle of generals and courtiers well rewarded, because if those insiders turn on him, he falls.

In 1986 Buchanan won the Nobel Prize for founding public choice, and Tullock, his co-author, was left out. Colleagues remember his bitter quip that co-writing The Calculus of Consent apparently did not count. The two had moved their Center for Study of Public Choice to George Mason University in 1983, where Tullock taught until 2008; he died in 2014.

hal-finney-first-node-first-transaction-.context_blurb:
When Bitcoin came to life in January 2009, almost nobody noticed. One of the few who did was Hal Finney, a California programmer who had spent two decades building tools for private communication and digital cash. He became Bitcoin's first partner, its first customer, and in the end one of its most moving witnesses.

Bitcoin was the creation of an unknown inventor who called himself Satoshi Nakamoto. It is money that exists only on computers and that no government prints; a worldwide network of computers solving math puzzles maintains the record of ownership that a bank would otherwise keep. Money of that kind, run by computers and cryptography, is called a cryptocurrency.

Finney was ready for it. For years his day job at PGP Corporation had been writing code for Pretty Good Privacy, software that scrambles a message so only the holder of the right secret key can read it. A government agency that intercepts such a message sees only gibberish, and that scrambling is called encryption.

He had also wrestled with digital cash himself. In 2004 he published a design called Reusable Proofs of Work, which he shortened to RPOW. Like other early digital-cash systems, it depended on one central trusted server, and that was its weak point: if that server is shut down or corrupted, the whole currency breaks.

Satoshi released the Bitcoin software in early January 2009, and Finney started it on his own computer a day or so after the network went live, making his machine the second Bitcoin node ever. On January 11 he tweeted just two words about what his machine was busy with: "Running bitcoin."

A day later Satoshi sent him 10 coins, the first time bitcoin had ever passed from one person to another. That small transfer mattered because it proved the new digital money actually worked the way its design promised.

Later in 2009 Finney learned he had amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, the disease that slowly paralyzes the body and is often called Lou Gehrig's disease. By 2013 he could type only by moving his eyes across a screen. That March, using eye-tracking software, he posted an essay on the bitcointalk.org forum titled "Bitcoin and Me," telling the whole story from the first node to his illness. He died in 2014, and, true to his lifelong interest in extending life, his body was cryopreserved by the Alcor foundation in Arizona.

Because he was there at the very start, Finney was often accused of secretly being Satoshi. Two lines of evidence rule it out. Finney denied it plainly himself, and the timeline does not fit: while Satoshi was busy sending emails, Finney was training for a marathon and posting his running times.

hazlitts-economics-in-one-lesson-bastiat.context_blurb:
Henry Hazlitt (1894-1993) was never a professor, yet his short book of 1946 has taught more Americans to think like economists than almost any textbook. A journalist all his life, he took one idea from a French pamphleteer of the 1840s and applied it to every policy of his own day.

The idea came from Frederic Bastiat. A rule must be judged by its effects on everybody, the hidden losers as well as the visible winners. Bastiat called it the method of what is seen and what is unseen, and Hazlitt preached it for twelve years in his New York Times editorials.

The essay Hazlitt carried forward was Bastiat's That Which is Seen and That Which is Not Seen, written in 1850 by a man dying of tuberculosis, months before his death.

Hazlitt's book was Economics in One Lesson, published in 1946 by Harper & Brothers. It has sold more than a million copies and has never gone out of print.

The method has one big lesson: always hunt for the hidden cost of a policy, not just the benefit everyone can see. The mistake it warns against is judging a policy only by the short-term help it gives one favored group.

Hazlitt put the rule in a single sentence. The art of economics, he wrote, is to trace a policy's consequences not just for one group and not just at the immediate moment, but for all groups and over time. Friedman and the congressman Ron Paul each recommended it as the first economics book a newcomer should read, and generations of American libertarians started there.

The same year, 1946, Hazlitt joined Leonard Read in founding the Foundation for Economic Education at Irvington-on-Hudson, often counted the first free-market think tank in the country; Read was its president and Hazlitt sat on its founding board.

From 1946 to 1966 Hazlitt also wrote the Business Tides column in Newsweek, and Milton Friedman, who later took a Newsweek slot of his own, called him the model. A magazine that keeps a writer for twenty years is itself a small lesson: readers can cancel any day and take their money elsewhere, so market competition keeps the editors working hard to please them.

In 1959 Hazlitt published The Failure of the New Economics, a reply to John Maynard Keynes that worked through the 1936 General Theory chapter by chapter and answered each argument in turn.

Friedrich Hayek admired the 1946 book, and his short verdict, a brilliant performance, has been printed on later editions.

ineptly-defended-the-line-sowell-borrowe.context_blurb:
In 1840s France, Frederic Bastiat wrote witty pamphlets defending free trade against a powerful protectionist lobby. He also left a rule about how to argue that writers still borrow today, the economist Thomas Sowell among them.

Bastiat warned that clever enemies are not a good cause's greatest danger. The worst thing that can happen to a good cause, he wrote, is not to be attacked skillfully but to be ineptly defended.

So he set himself a discipline. Nearly every essay in his 1845 collection Economic Sophisms first lays out the protectionist argument fairly, even sympathetically, in its strongest form, and only then answers it.

Today that move has a one-word name. Around 2010, writers in the online rationalist community, on sites such as LessWrong and Slate Star Codex, began calling it the steelman, in contrast to the straw man. A debate coach who tells students to restate a rival's idea as well as its own supporters would, before attacking it, is teaching steelmanning. The habit is worth building because it stops you from defeating a weak version of an argument while the strong version still stands.

The same essay shows Bastiat's other great habit, counting the unseen. When a town spends tax money on a new stadium, everyone sees the ribbon-cutting. Bastiat wanted the other side of the ledger counted: everything the taxpayers would otherwise have bought or built with that money, purchases and projects that now never happen.

Thomas Sowell, born in Gastonia, North Carolina, in 1930 and later a scholar at the Hoover Institution, has named Bastiat among the formative influences on his method. In 2000 he published Basic Economics, a plain-language guide to the whole field with no graphs or jargon; it went through five editions and sold widely to students and adults alike.

Sowell's 1987 book A Conflict of Visions applies the steelman to politics itself. It maps two rival worldviews: a constrained vision, in which human nature is flawed and wisdom lives in tested traditions, and an unconstrained vision, in which people can be perfected if the right experts are in charge. Sowell presents each in its strongest terms before tracing how they lead to different policies.

jekyll-island-the-secret-meeting-that-dr.context_blurb:
In November 1910 a few of the country's mightiest bankers, a senator and a Treasury official boarded a private railroad car in New Jersey and rode south to Jekyll Island, a millionaires' hunting club off the coast of Georgia. For about nine days they worked in secret, and what they wrote became the blueprint for the Federal Reserve.

They were drafting a central bank, an institution whose main job is to manage the nation's supply of money: how much money exists, and at what price it can be borrowed.

The party was led by Rhode Island's Senator Nelson Aldrich, who chaired the National Monetary Commission. With him came Paul Warburg of the investment house Kuhn Loeb, an expert on European central banks, Benjamin Strong of Bankers Trust and the Treasury official Piatt Andrew. Frank Vanderlip came as president of the National City Bank of New York, the bank tied to the Rockefeller fortune that later became Citibank. Henry Davison, a senior partner at J.P. Morgan and Company, drafted most of the written plan.

Secrecy was total. The men called one another by first names only so the staff would not learn who they were, kept the curtains drawn and said nothing in public for years. Their work became the Aldrich Plan of 1911. A plan like that becomes law only one way: Congress must pass it, and in modified form it did. President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act on December 23, 1913, creating America's first central bank since the Second Bank of the United States lost its charter in the 1830s.

Critics later raised one central worry. A money system that would shape the lives of every American had been designed by a few insiders, not in public. Public-choice economists put it more sharply: the bankers who would live under the new rules had drafted those rules themselves, a vivid case of regulatory capture at an agency's very birth.

Their wider lesson concerns who designs a central bank. The particular men who drew up the plan led the very New York institutions, and represented the very fortunes, that its structure would benefit, and they kept the whole trip secret.

The story stayed hidden for a quarter of a century. In 1935 Vanderlip finally told it in print, in an article for the Saturday Evening Post. He admitted that on that trip he had been as secretive, indeed as furtive, as any conspirator.

judy-shelton-the-austrian-tradition-fed-.context_blurb:
In 2020 the Senate fought over Judy Shelton, an economist President Donald Trump had picked for a seat on the Fed's Board of Governors, which runs America's central bank. The fight that followed was unusual. It turned on an old question that had not shaped a Fed nomination in decades: whether money should be tied to gold.

To see why, start with the gold standard. Until 1933 in America, and nearly everywhere before 1914, a citizen could swap paper money for a set amount of gold. A government could issue only as much paper as its gold could cover, so the rule stood guard against endless money printing.

Shelton had spent decades arguing for that kind of discipline. Critics and defenders alike placed her in the Austrian tradition and called her gold-standard-curious, a rare outlook for a Fed nominee. In her 1994 book Money Meltdown she warned that central banks were creating money far too freely, and she defined sound money as money that holds its value because no one can print it at will.

She had also called a bigger collapse early. In The Coming Soviet Crash, published in 1989, she argued that the Soviet economy would fail, which it did in 1991. The reasoning followed Friedrich Hayek: the planners in Moscow could never collect the countless facts about goods, prices and labor that a working economy depends on, the obstacle known as the knowledge problem.

Her writings had also questioned how far the Fed should stay independent of elected leaders. Many economists defend that independence for a plain reason: it keeps decisions about money from being bent to help one politician win the next election. Her doubts about the Fed's independence from the White House alarmed Democrats and some Republicans.

The resistance was fierce. Over a hundred people who had once worked at the Fed put their names to a public letter opposing her, and among the signers were seven former chairs and vice chairs of the Fed itself.

The Senate Banking Committee approved her, but in November 2020 the full Senate stopped her nomination, when Republicans Susan Collins, Mitt Romney and Lamar Alexander joined every Democrat to deny her a vote. Above all, the fight was about whether linking the world's money to gold is a respectable policy choice at all.

Austrian-tradition analysts read a public-choice lesson in her defeat. A candidate who openly proposes to constrain the institution she would join tends to be blocked by that institution's own alumni network.

Her warnings were being tested even while the Senate debated. In the first COVID lockdowns of spring 2020, the Fed pledged to purchase government bonds without limit, pouring new dollars into the economy. Austrian critics call that a hidden tax: the new money makes every existing dollar worth less, so savers quietly lose buying power.

katyn-1940-and-the-molotov-ribbentrop-pa.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1939 the two great dictatorships of Europe, which had spent years denouncing each other, suddenly made a deal. Within a year one of them had murdered much of a neighboring nation's leadership in secret, and then lied about it for half a century.

In Moscow on August 23, 1939, Vyacheslav Molotov and Joachim von Ribbentrop, the two foreign ministers, signed a non-aggression treaty for their governments: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. In public it promised peace between them. A secret protocol carved Poland, the Baltic states and part of Romania into German and Soviet spheres.

On September 1 Hitler's armies crossed Poland's western border, and the war in Europe began. On September 17 the Soviet Union invaded from the east, and the two powers divided the country between them. In June 1940 Moscow also annexed Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Stalin's secret police, the NKVD, then rounded up Polish army officers, policemen, priests, professors, teachers and lawyers. On March 5, 1940, the Soviet Politburo ordered them shot, and that April and May NKVD squads executed about 22,000 of these prisoners, in the Katyn Forest near Smolensk and at the prisons of Kalinin and Kharkiv, burying the bodies in mass graves.

The victims were chosen on purpose. A regime that wants to rule a conquered people goes after its educated class first, because officers, teachers and priests are the ones who could organize resistance to the new masters.

Taken together, the pact, the joint invasion, the seizure of the Baltics and the massacre establish a hard fact about the twenty-two months before Hitler turned on Stalin in June 1941. In those months the Soviet Union was not a neutral bystander but a co-belligerent of Nazi Germany.

After German troops found the graves in 1943, Moscow blamed the Nazis, and it kept telling that lie for almost half a century. On April 13, 1990, under Mikhail Gorbachev and his policy of openness, the Soviet government finally admitted that Soviet police had carried out the killings.

The last proof came after the Soviet Union itself was gone. On October 14, 1992, the Russian president Boris Yeltsin handed Polish leaders the secret Politburo file. The order of March 5, 1940, bore the signature of the man who had ordered the killings: Joseph Stalin.

In 2007 the Polish director Andrzej Wajda released a film called simply Katyn, told through the families searching for their missing men. The story was his own: Wajda's father, an army officer, had been among those shot at Kharkiv.

late-talking-children-1997-and-the-einst.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell is known for books on economics, race and history. But in the 1990s he wrote about something far from his usual subjects: bright children who start talking unusually late. The reason was in his own home, and the books ended up applying his economics to medicine.

Sowell's first rule of economics, the theme of the opening chapter of his plain-language textbook Basic Economics, is that every choice means giving up the best alternative you did not choose. A year at college costs a year of wages; a late movie costs sleep. Economists call that sacrifice the opportunity cost.

The new subject began with his son. Sowell's own son John was one of these children: specialists variously labeled the boy autistic, retarded or deaf, and all of them were wrong. John talked late and grew into a highly intelligent adult with a technical career.

Sowell gathered other families' stories and published Late-Talking Children in 1997. He saw a pattern: bright late talkers were often strong in math and music, and many came from families full of engineers, scientists and musicians. In 2001 he named the pattern after Albert Einstein, who, his family said, did not speak in sentences until about age three. He called it the Einstein Syndrome.

Sowell argued that the professionals who evaluate such children were not neutral judges. Pediatricians, therapists and school special-education offices, he said, had institutional incentives to sort children into named conditions, each with its own named treatment and its own funding stream, even when a particular child fit none of the labels.

This was Hayek's knowledge problem carried into pediatric medicine. No single specialist could see a pattern that crossed specialties, and the incentives inside each specialty rewarded intervention over patient waiting.

The same idea runs through Sowell's whole career. Big programs run by distant experts often make problems worse, he argued, not because the experts are wicked or insincere but because they are missing the detailed local knowledge held by the people on the spot.

ludwig-lachmann-radical-subjectivism-and.context_blurb:
Ludwig Lachmann (1906-1990) was born in Berlin, studied under Hayek in London and taught for some forty years in Johannesburg at Wits, the University of the Witwatersrand. He pushed one Austrian idea, that value and expectations live in individual minds, further than anyone, and he became the leading voice of what is now called radical subjectivism.

The starting point is the Austrian theory of value. What a thing is worth does not come from its materials or what it cost to make; it depends on who wants it, when and why. A cold bottle of water is precious in the desert and almost worthless in your fridge, and that is subjective value.

In 1956 Lachmann published a short, influential book, Capital and Its Structure. Lathes, delivery trucks and factory buildings are different tools with different uses that fit together in particular ways. Mainstream textbooks liked to add all of them up into one big number, called K, but Lachmann attacked the idea that capital can be squeezed into a single total, because the sum erases the very fit between tools that booms and busts disrupt.

He applied the same thinking to expectations. In the 1970s the school of rational expectations treated business owners as if they could calculate the future by probability. Lachmann, drawing on Frank Knight's 1921 distinction between measurable risk and true uncertainty, replied that the future is genuinely unknowable, so different entrepreneurs will reasonably form different expectations about it.

That has a sobering consequence. Dice have known odds, but the future holds inventions, companies and choices that do not exist yet, so no honest odds can be given. If Lachmann and the British economist George Shackle are right, a ten-year economic forecast is basically a guess and should not be trusted like a weather report.

His most radical statement came in a 1976 essay, From Mises to Shackle. Markets never settle into equilibrium; plans and expectations keep shifting, and the overall picture keeps rearranging itself, like the bits of glass in a kaleidoscope. Borrowing Shackle's word, he called this picture the kaleidic society.

He never doubted the school's core claim about planning. Mises, Hayek and their students argued that central planning fails not because planners are wicked but because the knowledge an economy needs is spread across millions of buyers and sellers, and no small group can ever collect it. Lachmann later taught at New York University, which under Israel Kirzner and Murray Rothbard became the training ground of the Austrian revival.

Lachmann also wrote The Legacy of Max Weber, in 1971. The German sociologist Max Weber had argued in his 1905 study of the Protestant ethic and the rise of capitalism that a culture's teachings, such as hard work, thrift and keeping your word, shape how its markets grow. His broad claim is that culture and shared habits shape a market as much as its formal rules do.

marginal-revolution-and-mru-cowen-and-ta.context_blurb:
George Mason University in Virginia became the home of public-choice economics when James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock moved their center there in 1983. A generation later, two of its economists carried the school's way of reasoning out of the seminar room and onto the internet.

They are Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok. Their blog, Marginal Revolution, at marginalrevolution.com, began in 2003, and they have posted on it every day for more than twenty years, which makes it one of the longest-running economics blogs online.

The tradition they inherited rests on a blunt idea, which Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel Prize for developing. People in government, from legislators to agency staff, follow incentives such as votes, larger budgets and promotions, as people everywhere do; they are not selfless guardians of the common good. That school is called public choice economics.

Taking the idea seriously changes how you read any political decision. A congressman or a judge is no angel once in office, so a politician will often pick whatever helps his or her own career rather than the general good.

In 2012 the pair opened Marginal Revolution University, a free online collection of short video lessons in economics. Its great gift is access: anyone with an internet connection can learn the subject without paying college tuition, and millions have enrolled, many of them home-schooled and high-school students.

Cowen also made an argument of his own. In his 2011 book The Great Stagnation he pointed out that the decades before the 1970s brought life-changing inventions such as electricity, the car, indoor plumbing and the airplane, while far fewer have arrived since. The result, he argued, is that productivity growth slowed, and with it the growth of the whole economy.

In 2015 Cowen launched an interview podcast in which he talks for about an hour with a single guest, from economists and historians to novelists, chess players and chefs. It is called Conversations with Tyler.

Their contribution to the Mason tradition is easy to name. Buchanan and Tullock built the academic structure; Cowen and Tabarrok moved its reasoning online and into the popular conversation about economics, through the blog, the free courses, the podcast and their textbook, Modern Principles of Economics.

minimum-wage-the-teenager-whose-job-is-p.context_blurb:
A minimum wage law sets the lowest hourly pay an employer may legally offer. Supporters see it as a raise for the poorest workers. Its critics, following the Frenchman Frédéric Bastiat's habit of hunting for the unseen, ask a harder question: what happens to the worker whose work is worth less than the floor? Milton Friedman, Thomas Sowell and Walter Williams spent decades asking it.

Picture a sixteen-year-old with no experience whose work is worth about eight dollars an hour to a small restaurant. If the law says fifteen, no owner can legally hire him at what he is worth, so his job never comes into being. Nobody fires him; he is simply never hired, and that is exactly why he is so easy to miss.

Friedman put the point bluntly in a 1966 Newsweek column and again in Free to Choose: a minimum wage law, properly described, orders employers to discriminate against people with low skills.

Seattle became a test case. Starting in 2015 the city phased in a fifteen-dollar floor, the highest in the country once it took full effect for big employers in 2017 and 2018. In those same years McDonald's, Panera and Wendy's spread self-order kiosks through their restaurants. A touch screen takes orders and draws no wage, so it becomes worth buying once the law makes cashiers expensive. Economists call this capital-for-labor substitution: when the law raises the price of workers, employers swap in machines that do the same work.

The most famous challenge to the critics came in 1994. David Card and Alan Krueger compared fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which had just raised its minimum wage, with restaurants over the line in Pennsylvania, which had not. They phoned managers, counted staff, and found little short-run loss of jobs on the New Jersey side. Their study became the standard citation for the claim that a wage floor need not cost jobs, and Card later shared the 2021 Nobel Prize for empirical work of this kind.

David Neumark and William Wascher answered that a manager's answer on the phone is a shaky measure. They collected payroll records, the hours each restaurant actually paid for, and in that data and in longer-run studies the job losses came back. Their 2008 book, Minimum Wages, pressed the case at length.

Thomas Sowell, in his textbook Basic Economics, argues that the real price is paid neither by the owner nor by the diner but by the chronically unemployed teenager, the young person whose first job never appears.

Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem gives the critics another edge. Lawmakers far away set one floor for a whole nation. The shop owner on the spot knows what each worker is really worth at that particular job in that particular town, and no statute written in the capital can know it for him.

Walter Williams, in Race and Economics (2011), anchored the debate in history. In the 1950s, when the federal floor was low in real terms, American teenage unemployment ran at about 10 percent. After repeated increases from the 1970s on, it averaged 15 to 20 percent in his account, and far higher among black teenagers.

Friedman, Sowell and Williams all closed their cases with the same rule, in Bastiat's spirit: judge a policy by its results, not by the good intentions of the people who sponsor it. The good a law intends is the seen; what happens to the unseen teenager is what counts.

misess-emigration-vienna-to-geneva-to-ne.context_blurb:
Ludwig von Mises was the leading free-market economist of Vienna between the two world wars and a fierce critic of every kind of socialism. As Hitler's power spread across Europe, Mises had to keep moving: first to Switzerland, then across a continent at war to America, where he spent the last three decades of his life.

Wherever he lived, he warned against inflation. A government that can print money whenever it likes, Mises argued, drives prices up and quietly drains the value of people's savings. And the system he defended, in Vienna, Geneva and New York alike, was free-market capitalism: private property and voluntary exchange guided by prices.

In 1934 Mises took a professorship at the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva. There he finished a large German treatise, Nationalökonomie, published in 1940, which he later rewrote and expanded in English as Human Action (1949). Appearing in a Europe already at war, the German book went almost unread.

Vienna was no longer safe for his work. When Nazi Germany swallowed Austria in the Anschluss of 1938, Gestapo agents searched Mises's empty flat and carted his private papers off to Berlin. At the end of the war Soviet troops seized those papers in turn and shipped them to Moscow, where they lay in a secret archive for about fifty years.

In the summer of 1940, as German armies overran France, Mises and his wife Margit left Geneva. They crossed a continent at war by bus to Portugal and sailed from Lisbon to New York, arriving in early August with almost nothing. Margit later told the story in her 1976 memoir, My Years With Ludwig von Mises, still the main firsthand source for the escape.

America gave him safety but not a job. No major university would hire him, and fellow Austrian exiles of the 1940s met the same cold welcome, because their ideas clashed with the Keynesian consensus that ruled the profession at the time.

New York University let him run a seminar from 1945 to 1969 with the title of visiting professor, but it paid him nothing. His salary came from private backers, the businessman Lawrence Fertig and the William Volker Fund. The arrangement shows a pattern worth noticing: private donors often pay for ideas that the academic mainstream will not support.

In Human Action Mises built all of economics on one fact that anyone can check in himself: people act on purpose, choosing means toward ends they value. He named the science of purposeful human action praxeology, a word built from Greek, and argued that every economic law follows from that starting point.

ncaa-amateurism-as-cartel-obannon-v-ncaa.context_blurb:
The National Collegiate Athletic Association, the NCAA, runs sports at more than a thousand American colleges. College football and basketball grew into giant businesses, worth billions of dollars a year in television deals and ticket sales. Yet for about a century the young players who drew the crowds were forbidden to be paid, until a string of court cases asked whether that rule was really a cartel.

The no-pay rule went by a noble name: amateurism. An athlete could receive a scholarship, room and board and a small stipend, but no wages for playing. So while schools, coaches and networks shared the billions, the players' cash share of all that money was basically none.

Economists saw something plainer than tradition. Any one school could have lured the best players by offering pay, yet all of them agreed, through the NCAA rulebook, that none would. An agreement like that is price-fixing among employers who ought to be competing for the same workers.

Ed O'Bannon, a former UCLA basketball star, was visiting a friend when he spotted himself, face and number and all, in a video game of college basketball. Millions of copies had been sold, and he had not been paid a cent. He sued, and his case rested on a basic property right: a person owns his own name and likeness, so a company that sells them owes him payment. In 2014 Judge Claudia Wilken ruled that the NCAA's limits broke antitrust law.

In June 2021 the Supreme Court decided the Alston case against the NCAA by a vote of nine to none, holding that its limits on the education benefits schools could offer athletes were illegal. A unanimous ruling carries special weight. When justices who usually disagree, named by presidents of both parties, all see a question the same way, the point is very hard to dismiss.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh added a concurring opinion that went further. He warned that "the NCAA is not above the law" and suggested that its whole amateurism system worked like an illegal cartel. A cartel is a group of firms that agree to fix prices or limit competition instead of competing; here the firms were schools fixing the pay of their players.

On July 1, 2021, college athletes at last became free to take money from sponsors for their name, image and likeness, known as NIL, and within three years those deals were worth over a billion dollars a year. One effect cut against the old fear that pay would empty the colleges. Some top players now stay in college longer, because they can earn real money there without turning pro.

The cracks had begun decades earlier. Until the 1980s the NCAA decided which college football games could be televised and how many. In 1984 the Supreme Court, in a case brought by the University of Oklahoma's regents, freed each school to sell the broadcast rights to its own games. Many more games went on the air, and over the following decades the television money for college football soared.

In June 2025 a federal judge approved the settlement of the House case, which lets each school share revenue directly with its athletes, roughly twenty million dollars a year per school. The settlement conceded a basic economic point: the people who create the value should be allowed to earn from it.

Economists in the public-choice tradition draw a general lesson. When an industry holds a key input far below its market price, by law or by custom, pressure builds against the rule that holds the price down, and sooner or later that legal or cultural prop gives way. Amateurism, dressed as noble tradition, held a star athlete's pay at zero for a century and then collapsed in about a decade once courts applied ordinary antitrust law.

north-koreas-public-distribution-system-.context_blurb:
For decades North Korea fed its people through the state rather than through shops. When that system broke down in the 1990s, a famine followed, and so did something the regime never planned: illegal markets that kept millions alive. The story shows both halves of the Austrian argument, what central planning cannot do and what free exchange does on its own.

Under the Public Distribution System, state outlets handed each family its grain, oil and other food. The ration depended on a person's job and on how loyal to the Party he seemed, so missing a rally could shrink a family's share. It was a government rationing system, and private trade in food was almost entirely banned.

Between 1993 and 1998 the system collapsed and famine swept the country. The state never called it a famine. It called it the Arduous March, a heroic name for a hardship everyone supposedly bore together, and a name like that hides who was to blame while it makes the disaster sound noble.

In 2007 the economists Marcus Noland and Stephan Haggard published Famine in North Korea. Piecing the toll together from interviews with refugees, crop readings from satellites and records of trade with China, they put the deaths at somewhere between 600,000 and 2.5 million, out of about 22 million people.

People still had to eat. On empty lots and in alleys, ordinary North Koreans began buying and selling food in defiance of the law, at first from baskets on bicycles. These illegal markets, the jangmadang, moved food from region to region and saved millions of lives.

Two young women who later escaped, Yeonmi Park and Hyeonseo Lee, described that world from the inside in memoirs published in 2015, including the long walks their families made to the markets for the rice the state never delivered.

When scholars mapped the deaths, they found hunger struck hardest in the northeastern provinces, the regions Pyongyang cut off from central grain shipments first, even though weather and sanctions were the same everywhere. The pattern shows that a failure of central distribution is itself a cause of famine.

Andrei Lankov, who was born in Russia and teaches history at Kookmin University in Seoul, has written more in English about the jangmadang than anyone, drawing on years of conversations with people who escaped.

The markets never went away. Surveys of escapees gathered by Seoul researchers suggest that about 70 to 80 percent of everyday consumption now flows through them, and the state tolerates them because the alternative is famine.

Austrian economists read the whole story as two of their arguments at once. The collapse of the rationing system is the calculation problem in acute form, since planners could not adapt when the aid vanished. The markets that rose without permission are Hayek's spontaneous order: people coordinating through prices that nobody designed.

oskar-morgenstern-from-mises-kreis-to-th.context_blurb:
Oskar Morgenstern grew up in the Vienna of the Austrian school and sat in Ludwig von Mises's private seminar in the 1920s. He ended his career at Princeton as a founder of one of the great new tools of the twentieth century. His life shows how an old Austrian question, how people act when each must guess what the others will do, turned into mathematics.

In 1928, still in Vienna, he published a study of economic forecasting and found a strange loop at its heart. Once a forecast is published, people react to it, and their reactions can make it come out wrong. That puzzle carries his name: Morgenstern's paradox.

In 1927 Mises had set up an institute in Vienna to study business cycles, with the young Friedrich Hayek, a future Nobel winner, as its first director. Their theory blamed one culprit for the cycle: when a central bank expands credit and drives interest rates below their natural level, it sets off a false boom that must end in a bust. When Hayek left for the London School of Economics in 1931, Morgenstern took over the institute.

In 1938 Morgenstern was lecturing in America when the Anschluss handed Austria to Nazi Germany. The new regime fired him from his Vienna post as politically unreliable, and he took up a chair at Princeton instead.

At Princeton he met John von Neumann, a Hungarian-American mathematician whose work ran from quantum physics to the bomb project at Los Alamos and the design of early computers. From 1940 to 1944 the two wrote a giant book together, with Morgenstern bringing the economic questions and von Neumann the mathematics.

Princeton University Press published it in 1944. Known for short as Theory of Games, with "and Economic Behavior" completing its full title, it founded game theory, which studies how people choose when each knows the others are trying to outguess him.

Morgenstern also spent decades warning that official statistics, such as gross domestic product and unemployment, carry far larger errors than the people steering policy admit. His book On the Accuracy of Economic Observations (1950) laid out the case in careful detail.

He always said game theory was a formal version of an old Austrian idea: economic outcomes emerge from the interplay of purposeful people, each choosing while anticipating the choices of others. In his eyes he had written the mathematics that Carl Menger and Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk never wrote.

physiocrats-and-classical-liberals-basti.context_blurb:
Years before Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations appeared, a circle of French thinkers was already arguing that governments should stop strangling trade. They were the Physiocrats, the first organized school of economists, and through later Frenchmen such as Jean-Baptiste Say their ideas passed down to Frédéric Bastiat.

They were led by François Quesnay, court physician to King Louis XV. The Physiocrats held that all real wealth springs from farming. In their doctrine of the net product, agriculture alone creates genuinely new wealth, because the land gives back more than is put into it, while crafts, trade and finance only reshape or move what the farms produce. Economists later rejected that claim, but the Physiocrats' case for free trade survived.

In 1758 Quesnay published the Tableau économique, a numerical chart tracing how the value of a harvest passed among farmers, landowners and artisans. It was the first attempt to picture the circulation of wealth through an entire economy, and it is often called the first economic model of a whole nation.

The motto of their circle was laissez faire, laissez passer, "let it be done, let it pass": leave people free to make things and free to move them, and let the government stand aside.

In 1774 their friend Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot became finance minister to the young King Louis XVI and tried to put the ideas to work. He moved to abolish the guilds that alone could practice trades such as baking, the corvée of unpaid road work forced on peasants, and the tolls that provinces charged on grain crossing between them. His aim was to let people work and trade more freely, so that the country would produce more. The privileged interests he threatened fought back, and in 1776 he fell from office.

Jean-Baptiste Say carried the tradition into the next century. In his Treatise on Political Economy (1803) he argued that production comes before spending: you can buy only with what you have made or earned.

English-speaking economists later squeezed his idea into a short slogan: supply, they said, creates its own demand. Making a chair or growing wheat generates the income that buys other goods in return. John Maynard Keynes attacked the slogan, while the Austrians defended Say's original point.

The spirit of the movement is older still. When Jean-Baptiste Colbert, Louis XIV's mighty finance minister, asked the merchant Le Gendre around 1680 what the crown could do for business, Le Gendre reportedly answered, "Laissez-nous faire": leave us alone. The phrase sums up the conviction that trade usually thrives when government interferes less.

ppp-loans-2020-the-concentrated-benefit-.context_blurb:
When the COVID-19 lockdowns began in March 2020, Congress passed the CARES Act, a relief package of about 2.2 trillion dollars, the largest in American history at the time. One of its programs, the Paycheck Protection Program, or PPP, offered small businesses loans that would be forgiven if they kept their workers on the payroll. It became a lesson in seeing both the seen and the unseen.

To a shop owner the money felt like a gift, but a government earns nothing by selling products. Every PPP dollar came from taxes and from borrowing that future citizens will have to repay.

The whole package was paid for with borrowed money, much of it absorbed by a Federal Reserve creating new dollars, while relief checks went to nearly every household. Over the next two years the predictable side effect arrived: sharp inflation, as everyday prices rose fast.

The MIT economist David Autor and his colleagues later used payroll records to measure what PPP achieved. They estimated that each job it preserved cost taxpayers about $170,000 to $257,000 for every year the job was kept, far more than the workers' own yearly pay.

They also asked where the money ended up. About 72 percent, they reported, went to business owners and shareholders rather than to workers, because most of the firms that received it would not have laid anyone off in the first place.

The rollout showed Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem at work. No central agency could know which of millions of firms truly needed help in April 2020, so the money flowed to whoever already banked with a big lender. Well-connected clients were funded in days, while many minority-owned and country businesses got nothing in the first round.

A second pandemic program offered a comparison. Extra unemployment benefits, $600 a week under the CARES Act, went only to workers who had actually lost their jobs, so for each job they protected they cost far less than PPP, which paid nearly every business whether it had lost customers or not.

A defender can point to the millions of owners who received forgivable loans, and a critic in Bastiat's tradition grants that those seen beneficiaries were real. The unseen cost is roughly $600 billion of public debt for firms whose employees would have kept their jobs anyway, a bill that future taxpayers now carry.

prices-as-knowledge-signals-the-core-aus.context_blurb:
Friedrich Hayek's short 1945 essay in the American Economic Review is the most cited text of the Austrian school. In eleven pages it answers a question that sounds simple and is not: how can an economy use knowledge that is scattered among millions of heads and that no planner could ever collect? Its answer is the price system.

Hayek's title says exactly what the paper is about: the use of knowledge in a society too large for any one mind.

Its central story is about tin. Suppose that somewhere in the world tin suddenly becomes scarce. Within days every user of tin is saving it, though no one has given an order and only a few people know the cause, because the rising price carries the message to all of them.

Most economists, Hayek said, made the same slip: they imagined a single wise planner who knew every fact. But the knowledge an economy runs on is dispersed. It never exists in one place, only as scattered and incomplete bits held by separate people.

Hayek called the person who holds such knowledge a man on the spot: the mechanic who knows this particular lathe, the shopkeeper who knows these particular buyers, the captain who knows this particular port. That knowledge of time and place cannot be written into a report and mailed to headquarters in time.

The essay was a reply. In 1936 and 1937 Oskar Lange had argued, in On the Economic Theory of Socialism, that a central planning board could play at markets: set prices, push them up when queues formed and down when goods went unsold. Hayek answered that the board would still lack the scattered knowledge that real prices gather.

Hayek's knowledge problem is the other side of Ludwig von Mises's 1920 calculation problem. Without market prices for factories, land and machines, Mises argued, socialism has no way to weigh what one production plan costs against another, such as whether a railway should be built of steel or of aluminium.

In 1974 Hayek won the Nobel Prize in economics, and the news startled people for an odd reason. He shared it with the Swedish economist Gunnar Myrdal, a social democrat whose views on central planning were nearly the opposite of his, and each spent his prize lecture disagreeing with the other.

In 1979 drivers across America again waited in lines around the block, buying gas only on odd or even days according to their license plates. In Hayek's terms the trouble was a federal ceiling on gasoline prices, left over from the 1973 controls, which broke the signal that would have called forth more supply. When President Reagan lifted the controls in January 1981, the lines soon vanished.

In 1980 Thomas Sowell stretched Hayek's essay into a full theory of how societies use knowledge, in markets, law, science and daily life. Hayek praised the result, Knowledge and Decisions, as the finest economics book he had come across in years.

Austrian economists apply the same argument to the biggest price of all. The interest rate, the price of having goods now rather than later, is not set by a market of lenders and borrowers but by a Federal Reserve committee that gathers eight times a year. In the Austrian view that committee holds it below the rate the market would set. That breaks the signal telling businesses which long projects real savings can support.

In 1948 Hayek gathered his key essays into Individualism and Economic Order, built around the 1945 essay and its forerunner, Economics and Knowledge, a talk he had first given to the London Economic Club in the 1930s.

public-sector-unions-fdrs-warning-and-wi.context_blurb:
Most Americans picture unions bargaining with private companies. Since the 1960s, though, the most heavily unionized workers in the country have been government employees, and economists in the public-choice tradition argue that bargaining with a government is a very different game. Even Franklin Roosevelt, a hero of the labor movement, saw the problem.

A strike at a shoe store hurts the owner, but customers can buy shoes down the street. If a whole city's police force went on strike on the same day, the people hurt most would be the ordinary citizens who need protecting, because nobody else can take the officers' place.

In 1937 Roosevelt wrote to Luther Steward, head of the National Federation of Federal Employees, that collective bargaining as usually understood cannot be carried over into government service, and he called a strike by public employees unthinkable and intolerable. Roosevelt, the champion of private-sector unions, opposed collective bargaining by government workers.

The difference, he explained, lies in who sits across the table. A private union faces a private employer out to make a profit, whose pay offers must be weighed against profits and the firm's survival. A government union faces officials spending other people's money.

By 2010 about 36 percent of government workers belonged to unions, against about 7 percent in private jobs, because public employees make up a compact, organized group while the taxpayers who foot the bill are scattered and unorganized.

In 2011 Wisconsin's new governor, Scott Walker, pushed through Act 10. Among other things it stopped the automatic deduction of union dues from public workers' paychecks and required unions to win a recertification vote every year, so that paying dues became each worker's own yearly choice rather than something taken from his pay without asking.

The fight was fierce. Weeks of protests filled the state capitol, and fourteen Democratic senators fled to Illinois, because without them the Senate lacked the quorum, the minimum number of members present, needed to pass Act 10. The walkout delayed the law but did not stop it.

Afterward the Wisconsin Education Association Council, the state's biggest teachers' union, saw a majority of its paying members leave within a few years. The drop suggests that many members had been paying only because the dues were taken automatically, not because they wanted to.

In 2018 the Supreme Court carried the voluntary principle nationwide. An Illinois state worker named Mark Janus objected to paying the "agency fees" that unions charged non-members, and on June 27 the Court ruled five to four in Janus against AFSCME that no public worker could be forced to pay them.

The cost of past bargains shows up in public pensions. CalPERS, the fund for California's state employees and the biggest public pension fund in the nation, manages about $460 billion, and its unfunded promises remain a long-term worry for the state.

Public-choice economists point to what sets government unions apart. A public union spends members' dues on campaigns to put governors and legislators in office, and then those same officials negotiate its contracts, so the union helps pick the officials who sit across the table from it.

When a union has helped choose its own bargaining partner, the usual picture of two independent sides breaks down. In effect the group is bargaining with itself, while the taxpayers who pay the bill have no seat at the table.

regulatory-capture-case-studies-icc-cab-.context_blurb:
Washington creates agencies to police powerful industries on the public's behalf. Again and again, though, economists have watched those agencies end up serving the very industries they were meant to restrain. The Chicago economist George Stigler gave the pattern its name in 1971, regulatory capture, and three old American agencies became its classic cases.

The first is the Civil Aeronautics Board. From 1938 the CAB assigned every airline its routes and fixed its fares, and flying stayed a luxury of the well-off. Then the Airline Deregulation Act, signed by Jimmy Carter in 1978, freed carriers to pick their routes and price their own tickets. Ticket prices dropped, and many more ordinary people could afford to fly.

Taking rules away from an industry in this way is called deregulation. Its champion at the CAB was the Cornell economist Alfred Kahn, who chaired the board in 1977 and 1978 and helped take it apart.

The oldest case is the Interstate Commerce Commission, created by Congress in 1887 to protect farmers and shippers from the railroads' rates. The historian Gabriel Kolko argued that the big railroads had themselves pushed for the ICC, hoping a friendly regulator would hold rates up and keep new lines out. That is regulatory capture: the industry ends up running its own regulator.

The Federal Communications Commission, created in 1934, hands out broadcast licenses, each a slice of the airwaves that no rival may legally use. License holders hired lobbyists to block new stations and to slow cable television for years, which shows how a license granted by government can become a protected privilege its holders fight to defend.

Deregulation spread. Two years after the airlines, the Motor Carrier Act of 1980 freed trucking, ending decades of ICC control over the rates and routes of the big rigs, and freight costs fell.

Capture has a familiar channel. An official oversees a drug maker for years, quits for a well-paid job at that company, and later someone from the company takes a post at the agency. People call this back-and-forth the revolving door.

Before the 2008 crash, the bank supervisors missed the risks piling up in mortgage lending. Post-crisis critics singled out the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which oversees national banks, and the Office of Thrift Supervision, which oversaw the savings-and-loans behind some of the worst mortgage books, pointing to staff who passed back and forth between those supervisors and the banks under their watch.

Why does capture happen so often? The most common reason is that the regulators come from the industry they oversee and expect to return to it, so they come to share its view. The Princeton political scientist Marver Bernstein had described the life cycle back in 1955: an agency is born full of zeal and grows old as the industry's partner.

The ICC, the CAB and the early FCC tell one story. In each case the industry's established firms captured the agency and used it to keep new competitors out.

Stigler said capture shows in outcomes, not intentions. The strongest visible sign is an agency that blocks new companies from entering while it protects the profits of the firms already there.

His 1971 paper, "The Theory of Economic Regulation," launched half a century of testing, much of it carried on by his student Sam Peltzman and their followers. In the reading of that Chicago tradition, study after study, from transport and broadcasting to banking and licensing, has largely vindicated the theory across every major agency examined.

ron-paul-end-the-fed-and-audit-the-feder.context_blurb:
Ron Paul is a Texas doctor who delivered babies before he went to Congress, where he served on and off from 1976 to 2013. No modern American politician did more to put Austrian economics before ordinary voters. His target, for four decades, was the Federal Reserve.

Paul's basic complaint was simple. The Fed can create new dollars whenever the government wants more to spend, and when it prints too many, each dollar buys less over time. Economists call that steady erosion of money's buying power inflation.

After the 2008 crash, which he blamed on the Fed, Paul wrote a book for general readers in September 2009. It became a best seller, and its title said it all: End the Fed.

On the House floor Paul built speech after speech on three Austrian economists, citing them constantly: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek and Murray Rothbard, who was also his personal friend.

As early as 2003 Paul told the House that house prices were swelling into a bubble that would end in a crash. He laid the blame on Alan Greenspan's low-rate policy: the Fed chairman, Paul said, had kept money cheap for years, and cheap money was inflating the bubble. Five years later the crash came.

In February 2009 Paul filed the Federal Reserve Transparency Act, which would have opened the Fed's books to a complete audit by Congress's own investigators at the GAO. At rallies and on signs the bill went by a three-word slogan: Audit the Fed.

The bill drew remarkable support. About 320 of the 435 House members signed on as co-sponsors before Senate leaders scaled it back to a one-time audit of the Fed's emergency lending, folded into the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

His book made three charges: that the Fed violates the Constitution, that printing money from nothing is morally wrong, and that it damages the real economy. For the economic charge Paul leaned on Mises and Hayek. The Fed, he argued, creates the very boom-and-bust cycles that Austrian business-cycle theory predicts, because artificially low interest rates lure businesses into mistakes that must end in a bust.

In 2011 the Mises Institute in Alabama gave him its highest award, named for his late friend: the Rothbard Medal of Freedom.

His constitutional case rested on Article I, Section 8, which gives Congress the power to coin money and regulate its value. In Paul's view that power belongs to Congress and cannot legitimately be handed over to an independent agency like the Fed, created in 1913.

Paul's biggest legacy is not a law but a shift in what counts as normal. Before his presidential campaigns of 2008 and 2012, criticism of the Fed lived on the fringes of politics; afterward, calls to audit the Fed or curb its powers became an ordinary position in Republican primaries.

sarbanes-oxley-2002-the-small-cap-ipos-t.context_blurb:
In 2002 Congress passed one of the biggest overhauls of American corporate rules in decades, named for its two sponsors in Congress, Michael Oxley of the House and Paul Sarbanes of the Senate. It was meant to stop the next great accounting fraud. Critics argue it also did something nobody intended: it made it much harder for small, young companies to sell shares to the public.

The trigger was Enron, the energy giant that hid enormous losses with accounting tricks and went bankrupt in 2001, wiping out thousands of workers' jobs and savings. After a scandal like that, lawmakers usually answer with new rules that force companies to prove their financial reports are honest.

Two collapses drove the law: Enron, the energy trader that failed in December 2001, and WorldCom, the phone company that failed the next summer, in July 2002, once its padded profits came to light. Sarbanes-Oxley was the response to Enron and WorldCom alike.

One section requires the chief executive and the chief financial officer of every large public company to sign, each quarter, a statement that the numbers are true, and a false signature can mean prison. The idea is to make real people legally responsible, so that no one can hide behind the company and claim he never knew.

Another section proved the most expensive to obey. Section 404 makes managers set up, test and personally vouch for a system of controls over their company's accounts, and it can cost even a small public firm one to two million dollars a year.

Over the following years many listed companies vanished, through mergers, buyouts or delisting, and fewer new ones replaced them. By the count of a widely cited study led by Gustavo Grullon, about 4,300 American companies remained listed by 2016, down from roughly 7,300 twenty years earlier.

The general lesson is about fixed costs. A bill of about a million and a half dollars barely dents a company earning billions but can sink one earning fifty million, so a regulation with a large fixed cost of compliance lands hardest on the smallest firms and shields the giants from newcomers.

Critics in Bastiat's tradition grant the seen benefit, fewer Enron-style frauds, and point to an unseen cost borne by ordinary savers. Promising young companies now stay private far longer, funded by venture capital and private equity, so retail investors have lost access to their early growth, which is reserved for wealthy accredited clients; the public can buy in only after most of the gains are gone.

self-custody-and-not-your-keys-not-your-.context_blurb:
Owning bitcoin is not like owning dollars in a bank. What you really own is the power to move coins, and that power is a secret. Twice in a decade, at Mt Gox in 2014 and at FTX in 2022, millions of people learned the hard way what happens when someone else holds that secret for them.

Every Bitcoin wallet rests on a secret number known only to its owner. With it, the owner signs a message proving he controls the coins, and the network accepts the transfer. That secret number is the private key: without it nobody can move the coins, however powerful he is, and anyone who steals it can move them all at once.

Most people buy bitcoin on an exchange and leave it there. But the exchange, not the customer, holds the private keys. If that exchange halts withdrawals or collapses, the customer discovers that all along he owned only a claim on the exchange, a promise to be paid in bitcoin, not the coins themselves.

The Bitcoin teacher Andreas Antonopoulos, author of the textbook Mastering Bitcoin (2014), drove the point home at conference after conference with a short rule: if they're not your keys, they're not your coins.

The safest storage is a hardware wallet, a small device, sold under brands such as Trezor, Ledger and Coldcard, that keeps the keys on a chip that never touches the internet. Its owner connects it only long enough to approve a payment on the gadget's own screen, so online hackers can never reach the keys.

If that device is lost or broken, a backup saves the day. The standard called BIP-39, written in 2013, lets an owner rebuild every key from twelve or twenty-four ordinary English words, all taken from one standard list of 2,048.

The first great lesson came in February 2014, when Mt Gox in Tokyo, then the biggest exchange in the world, halted withdrawals and went bankrupt, and about 850,000 customer coins vanished. Savers concluded that coins left on someone else's website can disappear whenever that company fails.

The lesson came again in November 2022, when the exchange FTX collapsed under its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, with billions of dollars of customer money gone. A New York federal jury convicted him of fraud, and in 2024 a judge gave him a 25-year sentence.

In both collapses, some customers lost nothing at all: those who had withdrawn to wallets of their own, holding the private keys themselves instead of leaving their coins with the exchange.

Careful holders go one step further with a multisig wallet, which splits the power to spend across several keys kept in different places. Coins can be spent only when enough of those keys agree, for example any two out of three, so no single stolen or broken device is fatal.

Bitcoin writers set Mt Gox and FTX side by side and press a definitional point. If you cannot sign for a coin, it is not your money in any meaningful sense; you own only a claim on whoever can sign, and you take the loss when he fails.

social-security-the-retirement-check-and.context_blurb:
Social Security, created in 1935, sends monthly checks to tens of millions of retired Americans. It is one of the most popular programs in the country. It is also a favorite case for economists who ask Bastiat's question: besides what the money does, what would it have done otherwise?

The very first monthly check went to Ida May Fuller, a retired legal secretary in Ludlow, Vermont, in January 1940. It was for $22.54, and she had paid in a mere $24.75 during her years of work. She lived to 100 and collected about $22,900 in all, because the first retirees paid in for only a few years while a huge generation of workers paid the taxes.

That points to how the system works. Today's workers pay the taxes that fund today's retirees; nobody's money is saved up for his own old age. In 1950 about sixteen and a half workers supported each person collecting, but with fewer babies and longer lives, by 2024 the number had fallen to about 2.7.

The law calls the payroll tax a "contribution," which sounds voluntary, yet anyone who refuses to pay can go to prison. Milton and Rose Friedman argued in Free to Choose that calling a forced tax a contribution disguises what is really going on, and that a private company advertising that way would be in trouble with regulators.

The courts agree about what the tax buys. Ephram Nestor, who came to America from Bulgaria in 1913, paid Social Security taxes for two decades. In 1956 the government deported him for his old Communist Party membership and stopped his benefits. Four years later the Supreme Court ruled that paying the tax buys no property right, and that Congress may change the benefits whenever it chooses.

Each year the program's trustees report when its reserve, the trust fund, will run out. In its 2025 report the depletion date arrived a year sooner than before: 2034. The law forbids the program to borrow, so once the reserves are gone, incoming payroll taxes would cover only about 81 percent of the benefits promised.

Other countries tried a different path. In May 1981 Chile, under the labor minister José Piñera, allowed workers to quit the government pension and put a tenth of their pay into a private retirement account. Switching was optional for those already in the old system, but workers within five years of retirement could not switch, since an account opened so late could not grow enough.

In January 2005 President George W. Bush made personal accounts his chief domestic goal, but Congress never voted on a bill. Support collapsed when voters concluded that the plan would cut the guaranteed benefit for everyone except the lowest earners.

A congressman can point to the 67 million Americans who receive a check each month. Critics in Bastiat's tradition accept the facts but call the defense incomplete. They demand a comparison with what forty-five years of the same payroll taxes would have grown into in each worker's own account. That comparison is contested, since a private account carries market risk and no built-in guarantees, which is why the argument is about the counterfactual rather than a simple verdict.
